lecture.title: Branches of Linguistics
lecture.scope: Lecture 2; original examples apply the definitions and distinctions taught in the supplied slides. One brief externally referenced definition explains the anthropological branch named on slide 4.
lecture.exam_alignment: Concept-based practice. No past paper or official examination blueprint was supplied.
lecture.answer_model: Single best answer. answer_id refers to an option id, not its displayed position. Preserve option ids when shuffling.
lecture.display_guidance: In learning mode, display explanation followed by example after the learner answers. Source slides and clarification notes can appear in a reference panel.

references.organization: Department of Anthropology, University of Toronto
references.title: Subfields
references.supports: Introductory identification of the language-and-culture focus of linguistic anthropology, a field named but not defined on slide 4.

clarifications.note: Micro/macro categories follow the slides when explicitly tested. They are not treated as universally fixed boundaries, and overlapping fields are distinguished by the stated research focus.
Although presented on a micro-labelled slide, lexicography is explicitly described there as dictionary compilation and a possible branch of applied linguistics.
The suffix -ly is adjective-forming in friendly. Questions do not generalize its function to every word ending in -ly.
Language acquisition is treated as a major psycholinguistic area. The slide’s unqualified ranking of it as the best-developed branch is not turned into an examination fact.
Computational linguistics studies natural language with computational tools and models. Programming languages may be tools. Merely using a computer does not make a project computational linguistics.
Brain damage is one source of neurolinguistic evidence, not a definition of the field’s entire scope. Behavioral difficulties are not treated as sufficient to locate a single brain region.
The overview’s label Anthropological is interpreted as the language-and-culture branch. Its brief introductory definition is externally referenced and clearly identified as clarification.

The slide’s wording about retrievable interpretations is explained as identifiable textual evidence and reasoning that readers can examine; it does not imply one mandatory response to a literary text.

topics.title: Phonology and its relationship to phonetics
Neurolinguistics and the brain basis of language

questions.question: What connects the different branches of linguistics introduced in this lecture?
questions.explanation: Linguistics studies language. Its branches ask different questions about structure, meaning, use, learning, and processing, while sharing language as their central subject.
questions.example: A researcher can study either sentence structure or language choice in a community as part of linguistics.

options.text: They all investigate spelling rather than speech.
They all concentrate on translating literary texts.
They investigate different aspects of human language.
They all prescribe a single correct accent.

questions.question: Which set consists entirely of microlinguistic branches in the classification used by these slides?
questions.explanation: The slides place phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics under microlinguistics. This is the lecture’s organizing scheme rather than a universal boundary between disciplines.
questions.example: Analysing how word parts combine falls under morphology in this scheme.

options.text: Phonology, sociolinguistics, and syntax
Syntax, neurolinguistics, and discourse analysis
Phonology, morphology, and syntax
Morphology, psycholinguistics, and stylistics

questions.question: Which set consists entirely of macrolinguistic fields as listed in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture groups these three fields under macrolinguistics. Each connects the study of language with broader questions about society, mental activity, or computation.
questions.example: Investigating how computers process natural language belongs to computational linguistics.

options.text: Computational linguistics, semantics, and phonetics
Psycholinguistics, syntax, and phonology
Sociolinguistics, morphology, and computational linguistics
Sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, and computational linguistics

questions.question: Which mapping follows the core-branch diagram in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The diagram organizes core branches by their main focus. These labels are a useful starting point, although a real research question can involve more than one level.
questions.example: Word endings suggest morphology, while the arrangement of words in a sentence suggests syntax.

options.text: Sounds: morphology; words: syntax; sentences: semantics; meaning: phonetics
Sounds: phonetics/phonology; words: morphology; sentences: syntax; meaning: semantics/pragmatics
Sounds: semantics; words: phonology; sentences: pragmatics; meaning: morphology
Sounds: syntax; words: pragmatics; sentences: phonetics; meaning: phonology

questions.question: A project measures pronunciation and relates its variation to speakers’ ages. How should its relationship to linguistic branches be understood?
questions.explanation: Branches describe areas of focus, not sealed compartments. Physical measurements can supply evidence for a question about socially patterned pronunciation.
questions.example: A researcher can measure vowel pronunciations and compare patterns across age groups.

options.text: It can combine phonetic analysis with a sociolinguistic research question.
It cannot be linguistic research because it crosses branch boundaries.
It must be phonetics alone because recordings exclude social questions.
It must be sociolinguistics alone because sound measurements cannot contribute.

questions.question: Why should questions about whether pragmatics is a micro- or macro-field specify the lecture’s classification?
questions.explanation: The slides place pragmatics under microlinguistics, but disciplinary groupings can vary. It is more useful to understand its subject than to treat a classification as an unchanging fact.
questions.example: Interpreting a speaker’s indirect request remains a pragmatic question whichever course heading contains it.

options.text: Every linguistics textbook uses exactly the same grouping.
The word “pragmatics” has no identifiable area of study.
Such groupings are teaching conventions, while the field’s focus remains language use in context.
Pragmatics becomes phonetics when it is grouped differently.

questions.question: Which question is most directly a phonetic question?
questions.explanation: Phonetics investigates speech sounds as produced by speakers, transmitted as signals, and perceived by listeners. It differs from questions about words, sentence structure, or social variation.
questions.example: A researcher might examine how a speaker’s tongue moves while producing a sound.

options.text: How are clauses combined into a sentence?
How are speech sounds produced, transmitted, or perceived?
How are dictionary entries selected?
How does language choice relate to social class?

questions.question: Which branch of phonetics studies the production of speech sounds in the vocal tract?
questions.explanation: Articulatory phonetics examines how the speech organs produce sounds. The focus is the speaker’s physical production rather than the transmitted signal or the listener’s perception.
questions.example: Studying how the lips close to produce /p/ is articulatory phonetics.

options.text: Articulatory phonetics
Acoustic phonetics
Phonology
Auditory phonetics

questions.question: A researcher observes where the tongue touches the roof of the mouth during a consonant. Which subfield is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The evidence concerns the position and movement of a speech organ. That makes the primary focus articulatory, even if recordings or other tools support the observation.
questions.example: Comparing tongue positions for two consonants investigates how they are produced.

options.text: Morphology
Articulatory phonetics
Acoustic phonetics
Auditory phonetics

questions.question: Which branch of phonetics studies the physical speech signal as it travels from speaker to listener?
questions.explanation: Acoustic phonetics concerns the physical properties of the speech signal. The vocal organs produce the signal, and the listener perceives it, but those are distinct points of focus.
questions.example: Comparing the duration of two recorded vowels is an acoustic investigation.

options.text: Auditory phonetics
Acoustic phonetics
Syntax
Articulatory phonetics

questions.question: A researcher measures the duration and frequency patterns of recorded vowels without investigating tongue movement or listener judgments. Which subfield is the best match?
questions.explanation: The measurements describe properties of the sound signal. Neither the production mechanism nor the listener’s response is the direct object of the analysis.
questions.example: A display of a recording can help compare how long two vowel sounds last.

options.text: Auditory phonetics
Lexicography
Acoustic phonetics
Articulatory phonetics

questions.question: Which branch of phonetics focuses on listeners’ hearing and perception of speech sounds?
questions.explanation: Auditory phonetics examines speech from the listener’s side. Acoustic phonetics examines the signal, while articulatory phonetics examines its physical production.
questions.example: Asking listeners which sound they heard can provide evidence about speech perception.

options.text: Acoustic phonetics
Auditory phonetics
Articulatory phonetics
Morphology

questions.question: Participants hear a series of similar speech sounds and report whether they hear /b/ or /p/. Which phonetic subfield most directly matches the task?
questions.explanation: The task records listeners’ perceptual responses. The experiment may manipulate acoustic signals, but the question asks specifically about what participants hear.
questions.example: A listener may classify an ambiguous sound differently from another listener.

options.text: Auditory phonetics
Lexicography
Articulatory phonetics
Acoustic phonetics

questions.question: Which sequence correctly matches three observations to the phonetic subfields: lip movement, properties of the recorded signal, and listeners’ sound identification?
questions.explanation: The sequence follows production, transmission, and perception. These are complementary perspectives on speech rather than three names for the same measurement.
questions.example: One project can observe lip closure, analyse the recording, and ask listeners what they heard.

options.text: Auditory, articulatory, acoustic
Acoustic, auditory, articulatory
Articulatory, auditory, acoustic
Articulatory, acoustic, auditory

questions.question: What is the main focus of phonology in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Phonology asks how sounds function together in a linguistic system. It examines patterns and relationships rather than only the physical properties of individual productions.
questions.example: Investigating which sound combinations a language permits is a phonological question.

options.text: The compilation of pronunciation dictionaries alone
The organization of sounds within a language’s sound system
The arrangement of paragraphs in written texts
The physical movement of the tongue alone

questions.question: A researcher investigates why some sound sequences are permitted in one language but not another. Which branch is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The question concerns language-specific sound patterns. It asks about the organization of the sound system rather than the mechanics of producing one sound.
questions.example: Two languages may allow different consonant sequences at the beginning of words.

options.text: Syntax
Lexicography
Articulatory phonetics
Phonology

questions.question: A student investigates whether exchanging two speech sounds changes word meanings in a particular language. Which branch provides the most direct perspective?
questions.explanation: The question concerns the functional role of sounds within a language. Meaning-distinguishing sound relationships are part of phonological organization.
questions.example: In English, replacing the first sound of “pin” with /b/ produces a different word, “bin.”

options.text: Morphology
Phonology
Discourse analysis
Acoustic phonetics

questions.question: Which comparison best distinguishes phonetics from phonology?
questions.explanation: The distinction is one of primary focus. Phonetic evidence can inform phonological analysis, so the fields interact rather than exclude each other.
questions.example: Measuring a vowel’s duration is phonetic; explaining its role in a language’s sound patterns is phonological.

options.text: Phonetics examines social class; phonology examines dictionary design.
Phonetics examines written words; phonology examines sentence order.
Phonetics examines speech production, signals, and perception; phonology examines sound organization in linguistic systems.
Phonetics examines word meanings; phonology examines literary interpretation.

questions.question: A study both measures consonant durations and asks how the consonants pattern in a language. Which description best fits the study?
questions.explanation: A measurement describes the physical speech signal, while a question about patterned linguistic organization is phonological. Using both perspectives is a coherent research design.
questions.example: Duration measurements can help investigate how a language organizes contrasting sound categories.

options.text: It cannot be phonology because physical measurements are included.
It becomes syntax because it compares more than one sound.
It becomes lexicography because all sound patterns belong in dictionaries.
It uses phonetic evidence to investigate a phonological question.

questions.question: Which pair of research questions keeps the analysis at the level of sound rather than word formation or sentence structure?
questions.explanation: The first question concerns phonetics and the second phonology. The alternatives move to morphological, syntactic, semantic, lexicographic, or discourse concerns.
questions.example: Tongue placement and permitted sound combinations are different questions about sounds.

options.text: How is a consonant produced, and which consonant sequences does a language allow?
What does a word mean, and how is a paragraph organized?
How is a plural word formed, and where does the subject occur?
How are dictionary meanings ordered, and how is an interview structured?

questions.question: What does morphology study?
questions.explanation: Morphology investigates internal word structure. Its units contribute meaning or grammatical information, so it differs from the study of speech sounds or whole conversations.
questions.example: Analysing “helpful” into “help” and “-ful” is morphological analysis.

options.text: How speech signals travel through the air
How words are constructed from smaller meaningful or grammatical units
How sentences form coherent conversations
How social class influences language attitudes

questions.question: The lecture analyses “friendly” as “friend” plus “-ly.” Which branch studies this construction?
questions.explanation: The analysis divides a word into meaningful parts and explains how the parts combine. It is about word structure rather than the ordering of separate words in a sentence.
questions.example: “Kindness” can similarly be analysed as “kind” plus “-ness.”

options.text: Morphology
Discourse analysis
Phonology
Syntax

questions.question: What role does “-ly” have in the lecture’s example “friendly”?
questions.explanation: In “friendly,” the suffix contributes to forming an adjective from a noun. Its role in this example should be identified from the actual word, rather than assuming that every “-ly” form is an adverb.
questions.example: In “a friendly neighbor,” “friendly” describes the neighbor.

options.text: It places “friend” into the past tense.
It changes the sentence from a statement into a question.
It combines with “friend” to form an adjective.
It combines with “friend” to mark a plural noun.

questions.question: Which comparison correctly distinguishes morphology from syntax?
questions.explanation: Both fields investigate linguistic structure, but at different primary levels. Morphology focuses on the makeup of a word, while syntax focuses on combinations of words.
questions.example: “Unhelpful” has internal word structure; “The student was helpful” has sentence structure.

options.text: Morphology examines social identities; syntax examines brain injuries.
Morphology examines paragraph links; syntax examines dictionary selection.
Morphology examines structure within words; syntax examines how words form larger structures.
Morphology examines listeners’ hearing; syntax examines sound transmission.

questions.question: A researcher asks what grammatical information the ending contributes in “books” compared with “book.” Which branch is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The question concerns an ending within a word and the grammatical information it contributes. This directly matches the lecture’s description of smaller units with grammatical functions.
questions.example: The ending “-s” in “books” marks more than one book.

options.text: Literary stylistics
Acoustic phonetics
Morphology
Pragmatics

questions.question: Which question is morphological rather than phonetic?
questions.explanation: The correct question asks about a meaningful part of a word. The alternatives examine the signal, articulation, or perception of sounds, which are phonetic concerns.
questions.example: In “unhappy,” “un-” contributes a negative meaning to the base “happy.”

options.text: Where does the tongue move during the first vowel of “unhappy”?
How long does the vowel last in a recording of “unhappy”?
Which sound does a listener identify at the start of “unhappy”?
What meaning does the prefix contribute in “unhappy”?

questions.question: Which activity defines lexicography in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Lexicography concerns making dictionaries. It involves decisions about entries and the information users need about words, rather than only investigating one structural level of language.
questions.example: Preparing definitions and examples for a learner’s dictionary is lexicographic work.

options.text: Investigating language processing after brain damage
Compiling dictionaries
Measuring speech signals
Modelling sentence structure

questions.question: An editor decides which words to include in a learner’s dictionary and writes clear definitions with usage examples. Which field is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The editor is constructing a dictionary resource. Meaning and grammar can inform the work, but the practical focus on dictionary entries makes lexicography the best answer.
questions.example: The editor may add a sample sentence to show how a difficult word is used.

options.text: Auditory phonetics
Syntax
Neurolinguistics
Lexicography

questions.question: How should lexicography’s position in the slides be interpreted?
questions.explanation: A slide’s location does not override its definition. The lecture explicitly connects lexicography with applied linguistics, so questions should preserve that qualification.
questions.example: A learner’s dictionary can apply research on meaning and grammar to a practical reference tool.

options.text: It is introduced beside micro-fields, but the slide also identifies dictionary compilation as an applied activity.
It is another name for the study of sound patterns.
It must study sounds only because it appears near morphology.
It cannot use linguistic analysis because dictionaries are practical resources.

questions.question: Which distinction best separates a lexicographic task from a primarily semantic research question?
questions.explanation: The fields can overlap because dictionary makers need knowledge of meaning. The difference here is the goal: producing a dictionary entry versus investigating meaning itself.
questions.example: Research on the meanings of “bank” can inform separate senses in a dictionary entry.

options.text: Choosing dictionary entries is syntactic; arranging words into clauses is lexicographic.
Designing a dictionary entry is lexicographic; investigating a word’s meaning relationships is semantic.
Studying meaning is unrelated to preparing useful dictionary entries.
Writing a definition is phonetic; measuring word meaning is articulatory.

questions.question: Which branch investigates the rules governing how words combine into sentences?
questions.explanation: Syntax studies sentence structure and the organization of words into larger units. It is concerned with how a sentence is formed, rather than just with the parts inside a word.
questions.example: The ordering of subject and verb is a syntactic concern.

options.text: Lexicography
Syntax
Acoustic phonetics
Morphology

questions.question: A student investigates why “The child has arrived” is a well-formed ordinary English statement but “Child the arrived has” is not. Which branch is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The words are arranged differently, so the central issue is their structural combination. The contrast does not require a change in vocabulary or pronunciation.
questions.example: Knowing word meanings alone does not tell a learner how to arrange “has,” “she,” and “left.”

options.text: Sociolinguistics
Lexicography
Phonetics
Syntax

questions.question: A researcher compares how English and Urdu arrange subjects, objects, and verbs. Which branch most directly addresses this question?
questions.explanation: The comparison concerns word arrangement and grammatical relationships within sentences. It therefore belongs primarily to syntax, even though other aspects of the languages may also differ.
questions.example: Comparing where the verb appears in equivalent sentences is a syntactic comparison.

options.text: Syntax
Morphology
Lexicography
Acoustic phonetics

questions.question: Which task is syntactic rather than morphological?
questions.explanation: The syntactic task concerns how separate words combine into a larger unit. The alternatives concern parts within individual words, which are morphological questions.
questions.example: Analysing the structure of “those two books” investigates a phrase rather than a suffix.

options.text: Explaining how “help” and “-ful” form “helpful”
Explaining the plural ending in “students”
Explaining how the words in “the very helpful student” form a phrase
Explaining the negative prefix in “unhelpful”

questions.question: Why does a study of sentence structure need to examine more than the meanings of individual words?
questions.explanation: The same words can participate in different relationships when their arrangement changes. Syntax helps explain that organization, while semantics examines the meanings involved.
questions.example: “The dog chased the cat” and “The cat chased the dog” use the same main words but assign different roles.

options.text: Grammatical relationships depend partly on how words are organized together.
Sentence structure is determined solely by how loudly words are spoken.
Dictionary order determines the grammatical role of every word.
Every word loses its meaning as soon as it enters a sentence.

questions.question: Which research question is primarily about syntax rather than semantics?
questions.explanation: The correct question asks about the placement of a grammatical element in sentence structure. The alternatives focus on meaning relationships and reference.
questions.example: Comparing “She is ready” with “Is she ready?” draws attention to structural organization.

options.text: Where can an auxiliary occur when an English question is formed?
Which objects can the word “vehicle” refer to?
How are the meanings of “large” and “big” related?
What meanings distinguish two senses of “bank”?

questions.question: What does semantics study according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: Semantics investigates linguistic meaning. It can examine words and whole sentences, including their relation to objects and situations that are real or imagined.
questions.example: Asking what “vehicle” means is a semantic question.

options.text: The selection of fonts for dictionary entries
The physical transmission of speech sounds alone
The social distribution of pronunciation alone
Meaning, including how words and sentences relate to what they refer to or describe

questions.question: A researcher investigates how the meanings of “large” and “big” are related. Which branch is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The question concerns a relationship between word meanings. It is not primarily about how the words sound or where they occur in a sentence.
questions.example: Comparing the meanings of “small” and “little” is another semantic investigation.

options.text: Phonetics
Syntax
Semantics
Neurolinguistics

questions.question: Why can the meaning of a sentence about a dragon still be studied in semantics?
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly includes real or imaginary referents. A sentence can be meaningful and interpretable without describing something that exists in the actual world.
questions.example: “The dragon guarded the tower” describes an understandable fictional situation.

options.text: Every sentence about fiction belongs exclusively to phonetics.
An imaginary subject removes all possible linguistic meaning.
Semantic analysis can examine reference to imaginary entities as well as real ones.
Semantics studies only sentences whose subjects are visible.

questions.question: A student asks how “The child opened the door” differs in meaning from “The child closed the door.” Which branch most directly addresses the difference?
questions.explanation: Both sentences have a similar grammatical pattern, but they describe different events. The immediate comparison is about what the sentences mean.
questions.example: “The lamp is on” and “The lamp is off” also differ in the situations they describe.

options.text: Semantics
Acoustic phonetics
Discourse analysis
Lexicography

questions.question: Which question focuses on conventional linguistic meaning rather than a particular speaker’s contextual intention?
questions.explanation: The first question centres on the meaning encoded by an expression. The alternatives ask how a speaker uses that expression for a purpose in a specific interaction, which foregrounds pragmatics.
questions.example: Understanding “closed” differs from inferring why someone chose to announce that a shop is closed.

options.text: Why did the speaker mention the closed shop to discourage a journey?
Was the speaker indirectly asking the listener to leave?
What does “closed” mean in the sentence “The shop is closed”?
Did the listener interpret the remark as a complaint about opening hours?

questions.question: Which comparison separates a syntactic question from a semantic question?
questions.explanation: Sentence organization and sentence meaning are related but distinguishable concerns. A complete analysis may investigate both without treating them as identical.
questions.example: For “The girl opened the window,” one can analyse the subject–verb–object arrangement and the event described.

options.text: Syntax asks how loud speech is; semantics asks where the tongue moves.
Syntax asks about social class; semantics asks about the age of a speaker.
Syntax asks how a sentence is structured; semantics asks what situation it describes.
Syntax asks who wrote a dictionary; semantics asks how its pages are numbered.

questions.question: Which branch most directly investigates how context affects the interpretation of an utterance?
questions.explanation: Pragmatics studies language use in communication. Time, place, participant relationships, and shared assumptions can influence what a speaker communicates.
questions.example: A remark about a cold room can function as a request when the window is open.

options.text: Morphology
Lexicography
Acoustic phonetics
Pragmatics

questions.question: Beside an open window, a student says “It is cold in here” to get a classmate to close it. Which branch most directly studies this intended request?
questions.explanation: The utterance literally describes temperature, but the context supports an additional intention. Pragmatics examines how the listener infers that intended use.
questions.example: At a crowded table, “There is no space here” may similarly imply a request to move something.

options.text: Semantics
Morphology
Phonology
Pragmatics

questions.question: A researcher asks why a student uses a more formal request with a lecturer than with a close friend. The focus is how the relationship shapes the intended request. Which branch is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The lecturer–student or friendship relationship contributes to the interpretation and formulation of the request. This fits the lecture’s inclusion of social relationships within pragmatic context.
questions.example: “Could you please help me?” may suit a situation in which a speaker wants to show respect.

options.text: Lexicography
Acoustic phonetics
Pragmatics
Morphology

questions.question: Different speakers say “I will meet you here tomorrow” in different places and on different days. Which branch studies how these circumstances determine the intended references?
questions.explanation: Identifying the intended people, place, and day requires information about the utterance situation. The words alone do not name the same participants and location in every use.
questions.example: “Here” can refer to a classroom in one conversation and a station in another.

options.text: Pragmatics
Articulatory phonetics
Morphology
Lexicography

questions.question: A speaker says “The usual place?” expecting a friend to identify a familiar café. Which aspect of context is most important?
questions.explanation: The speaker relies on common experience rather than naming the café. Pragmatics examines how assumptions about what the listener knows support communication.
questions.example: Friends may understand “our teacher” without a name when they know which class is being discussed.

options.text: The speaker’s assumption that the listener shares relevant knowledge
The alphabetical position of “usual” in a dictionary
The internal word structure of “place”
The physical duration of each vowel in the question

questions.question: Which pair correctly separates a semantic focus from a pragmatic focus?
questions.explanation: Meaning encoded in an expression and the communicative purpose of using it are different analytical concerns. They can both matter to understanding the same utterance.
questions.example: A learner can know what “late” means yet miss that a teacher’s remark expresses dissatisfaction.

options.text: The conventional meaning of “late” is syntactic; a complaint is phonological.
The conventional meaning of “late” is semantic; why a speaker calls someone “late” as a complaint is pragmatic.
The conventional meaning of “late” is acoustic; a complaint is morphological.
The position of “late” in a dictionary is pragmatic; the duration of its vowel is semantic.

questions.question: Why is the same sentence not guaranteed to communicate the same intended message in every situation?
questions.explanation: The linguistic form contributes meaning, but its use can depend on circumstances. A listener may infer a warning, request, criticism, or neutral report from the same wording.
questions.example: “There is a car coming” can report traffic or warn someone about to step into the road.

options.text: Sentence structure prevents speakers from implying anything beyond a literal description.
Dictionary definitions make interpretation independent of participants.
Its sound units automatically change meaning whenever the speaker moves.
Context and assumptions about participants can change what the speaker is doing with it.

questions.question: Which project foregrounds pragmatics rather than sociolinguistic patterns across groups?
questions.explanation: The first project focuses on interpreting a communicative act in context. The alternatives foreground the social distribution of language forms, choices, or attitudes. The fields may still overlap.
questions.example: Understanding “Can you reach the salt?” as a request foregrounds pragmatic interpretation.

options.text: Measuring which languages different occupational groups use most often
Investigating attitudes toward regional varieties across a city
Explaining how a listener infers an indirect request from one utterance in its immediate situation
Comparing pronunciation patterns across age groups

questions.question: What is the central concern of sociolinguistics in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Sociolinguistics studies how language relates to social life. The lecture includes social class, education, age, sex, ethnic origin, language choice, planning, and attitudes.
questions.example: A study might ask whether different age groups favor different expressions.

options.text: The physical production of individual sounds alone
Relationships between language and social factors
The placement of words in isolated sentences alone
The design of word entries in dictionaries alone

questions.question: A researcher compares vocabulary choices among younger and older speakers in Lahore. Which branch is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The question relates language use to age as a social factor. The location provides a setting, but the central comparison is between groups of speakers.
questions.example: Researchers might compare the use of a recent slang term across age groups without assuming that age determines every individual’s choice.

options.text: Lexicography
Neurolinguistics
Sociolinguistics
Syntax

questions.question: Bilingual speakers report when they choose Punjabi, Urdu, or English in different community settings. Which field most directly studies this pattern?
questions.explanation: Language choice in multilingual communities is explicitly included in the lecture’s account of sociolinguistics. The issue concerns who uses which language and in what social circumstances.
questions.example: A speaker might use one language at home and another in a formal meeting.

options.text: Lexicography
Articulatory phonetics
Morphology
Sociolinguistics

questions.question: Participants rate some accents as more prestigious than others. A researcher investigates these judgments as social attitudes. Which branch is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The research concerns beliefs and evaluations attached to language varieties. It studies the social attitudes themselves rather than assuming that an accent is inherently superior.
questions.example: A community may associate a variety with education, even though that association is a social judgment.

options.text: Syntax
Acoustic phonetics
Morphology
Sociolinguistics

questions.question: A team investigates which languages a multilingual community uses before advising on public-service language provision. Which pairing best describes the work?
questions.explanation: The investigation concerns community language use, while the advice addresses a practical policy problem. Sociolinguistics and applied linguistics can therefore contribute to the same project.
questions.example: Survey findings could inform which language versions of a public notice are needed.

options.text: Acoustic investigation contributing to automatic speech recognition
Psycholinguistic investigation contributing to a language-learning programme
Sociolinguistic investigation contributing to an applied language-planning task
Morphological investigation contributing to a learner’s dictionary

questions.question: A researcher finds an association between education level and a pronunciation pattern. Which interpretation is most careful?
questions.explanation: Sociolinguistic findings describe relationships that need evidence and context. An association does not justify an absolute prediction about every person or a ranking of groups as linguistically inferior.
questions.example: Two speakers with the same education level may still use different pronunciations.

options.text: Education alone necessarily determines every individual’s pronunciation.
The pattern proves that one group’s language has no grammar.
A social association makes any further analysis of language unnecessary.
The result describes a pattern in the sampled speakers and requires interpretation in its social context.

questions.question: Which set contains social factors explicitly included in the lecture’s description of sociolinguistics?
questions.explanation: The listed factors describe dimensions of social grouping in the slide. They can be investigated in relation to language without assuming that all members of a group speak alike.
questions.example: A study can compare patterns across age groups while also recording participants’ educational backgrounds.

options.text: Prefixes, suffixes, roots, word endings, and word classes
Vowel duration, signal frequency, sound intensity, tongue position, and lip closure
Dictionary entries, headwords, page numbers, definitions, and cross-references
Social class, educational level, age, sex, and ethnic origin

questions.question: What is the main focus of discourse analysis as introduced in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Discourse analysis examines connected language. Its focus goes beyond isolated words or sentences to how stretches of spoken or written language work together.
questions.example: An interview contains linked questions and answers that can be studied as a larger interaction.

options.text: How the tongue produces a single consonant
How dictionary headwords are alphabetized
How a suffix changes an individual word
How language forms larger meaningful units such as paragraphs, conversations, and interviews

questions.question: A student investigates how several sentences develop one argument across a paragraph. Which branch is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The student asks how sentences contribute to a larger meaningful whole. Analysing the paragraph as connected language makes discourse analysis the best answer.
questions.example: One sentence may introduce a claim while the following sentences explain and support it.

options.text: Articulatory phonetics
Discourse analysis
Morphology
Lexicography

questions.question: A researcher studies how interview questions shape the sequence of answers and follow-up questions. Which field most directly fits this focus?
questions.explanation: The object of analysis is the organization of a stretch of interaction. The researcher examines how contributions relate across the interview rather than analysing words in isolation.
questions.example: A short answer can lead an interviewer to ask for clarification in the next turn.

options.text: Discourse analysis
Lexicography
Phonology
Morphology

questions.question: Which distinction best separates the lecture’s introductory accounts of syntax and discourse analysis?
questions.explanation: The fields differ in their main unit and question, although they can interact. Discourse analysis can investigate both spoken and written material.
questions.example: A clause’s word order is a syntactic concern; how that clause responds to an earlier question is a discourse concern.

options.text: Syntax studies word definitions; discourse analysis studies sound transmission.
Syntax foregrounds sentence structure; discourse analysis foregrounds connected stretches of language.
Syntax studies all social groups; discourse analysis studies the vocal organs.
Syntax studies speech only; discourse analysis studies writing only.

questions.question: Which set could all serve as data for discourse analysis under the lecture’s definition?
questions.explanation: Each item contains connected language whose parts can contribute to a larger meaning or interaction. Discourse analysis is not restricted to formal written paragraphs.
questions.example: A recorded conversation and a written interview can both be examined for how their parts connect.

options.text: A prefix list, a suffix list, and a list of roots
A paragraph, a conversation, and an interview
A tongue-position diagram, a vowel waveform, and a lip-motion image
A dictionary’s page size, binding type, and printing cost

questions.question: What does stylistics investigate in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Stylistics asks how choices in language contribute to a particular style or effect. It can examine choices made by individuals or social groups in specific situations.
questions.example: A public notice and a friendly message may use different wording to suit different purposes.

options.text: Linguistic choices and variation in relation to situation and intended effects
The identification of all words with the same ending
The physical hearing of sounds without considering language choices
The location of language functions in brain tissue

questions.question: A researcher compares an advertisement’s short sentences and vivid vocabulary with a formal report to explain their different effects on readers. Which branch is foregrounded?
questions.explanation: The analysis connects identifiable language choices with style and communicative effect. It does more than label one text as interesting or another as formal.
questions.example: An advertisement may repeat a short phrase to make its message memorable.

options.text: Auditory phonetics
Neurolinguistics
Stylistics
Lexicography

questions.question: A speaker chooses brief, repeated phrases to make a public address sound urgent. Which research question is most directly stylistic?
questions.explanation: A stylistic question links features of the wording to the effect the speaker seeks. Physical measurement, perception, and automatic transcription ask different primary questions.
questions.example: Repeating “Act now” may create urgency, which the analyst should support with evidence from the speech.

options.text: Which software converts the recording into a written transcript?
Which participants have difficulty hearing the speech?
How do the chosen phrases and repetition contribute to the sense of urgency?
How long does each vowel last in milliseconds?

questions.question: Which focus most clearly foregrounds stylistics rather than a sociolinguistic survey of group differences?
questions.explanation: The first focus connects textual choices with style and effect. The other questions foreground social distribution or attitudes. These interests can overlap in broader research.
questions.example: Examining how a notice achieves an impersonal tone is a stylistic analysis.

options.text: Comparing which regional accents listeners rate most favorably
Explaining how a writer’s sentence and vocabulary choices create a formal tone in a particular text
Investigating language choice across occupational groups
Comparing age groups’ reported use of a local variety

questions.question: What makes literary stylistics distinct within the lecture’s account of stylistics?
questions.explanation: Literary stylistics uses evidence from linguistic form to support interpretations of literature. The lecture includes fiction, drama, and poetry among the genres that can be compared.
questions.example: An analyst can examine repeated sentence patterns in a poem to support an interpretation.

options.text: It applies linguistic methods to the interpretation and comparison of literary texts.
It replaces all textual evidence with a reader’s personal preference.
It deals only with the physical printing of novels.
It evaluates literature without examining its language.

questions.question: A researcher analyses sound repetition, word choices, and sentence patterns in a poem to explain its effect. Which field is the most direct match?
questions.explanation: The object is a literary text, and the method connects linguistic evidence to interpretation. Several linguistic levels may contribute to one literary stylistic analysis.
questions.example: Repeated sounds may reinforce a pattern that also appears in the poem’s vocabulary.

options.text: Language planning
Lexicography
Neurolinguistics
Literary stylistics

questions.question: Which approach best supports the lecture’s aim of making literary interpretations retrievable and comparable?
questions.explanation: An interpretation is easier to assess when readers can locate the evidence and follow the reasoning. Linguistic analysis can make that reasoning explicit without requiring identical responses from all readers.
questions.example: An analyst can point to repeated questions in a dramatic speech and explain their contribution to uncertainty.

options.text: State that a poem feels powerful without identifying any textual features.
Assume that every reader must respond identically to each sentence.
Identify specific linguistic patterns and show how they support the proposed interpretation.
Rank texts only by the personal reputation of their authors.

questions.question: Which field studies mental processes involved in planning, producing, perceiving, and understanding language?
questions.explanation: Psycholinguistics investigates language as a mental activity. It asks how users learn, produce, and understand language, rather than limiting itself to the outward forms of sentences.
questions.example: A researcher may investigate how a listener retrieves the meaning of a familiar word.

options.text: Literary stylistics
Lexicography
Sociolinguistics
Psycholinguistics

questions.question: An experiment investigates how memory demands affect a listener’s understanding of long sentences. Which field is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The question connects comprehension with a mental resource: memory. The lecture explicitly gives memory limitations as an example of a psycholinguistic concern.
questions.example: A listener may struggle to retain the beginning of a sentence while processing a long continuation.

options.text: Psycholinguistics
Sociolinguistics
Lexicography
Articulatory phonetics

questions.question: A researcher tracks how children learn to produce and understand their first language. Which field named in the lecture directly includes this area?
questions.explanation: Language acquisition is a major area discussed under psycholinguistics in the lecture. The study concerns the development of linguistic knowledge and processing abilities.
questions.example: A researcher may record changes in a child’s word combinations over several months.

options.text: Literary stylistics
Acoustic phonetics
Lexicography
Psycholinguistics

questions.question: A study investigates how speakers select words and plan an utterance before saying it. Which field is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The primary question concerns mental processes of language production. A conversation could provide data, but the focus is planning an utterance rather than organizing the exchange as a whole.
questions.example: A speaker may pause while retrieving a word needed to complete a message.

options.text: Psycholinguistics
Sociolinguistics
Lexicography
Discourse analysis

questions.question: Which distinction best separates psycholinguistics from neurolinguistics at the introductory level?
questions.explanation: The fields overlap because mental processing is supported by the brain. The distinction is the primary explanatory focus, not an absolute separation between unrelated subjects.
questions.example: A memory-load task foregrounds processing; relating language performance to brain damage foregrounds the neural basis.

options.text: Psycholinguistics excludes comprehension; neurolinguistics excludes production.
Psycholinguistics studies writing only; neurolinguistics studies speech only.
Psycholinguistics foregrounds mental language processes; neurolinguistics foregrounds their brain basis.
Psycholinguistics studies social class; neurolinguistics studies dictionary entries.

questions.question: What is the main concern of applied linguistics in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Applied linguistics connects knowledge about language with real needs. The lecture includes teaching, policy, translation, advertising, classrooms, and legal contexts.
questions.example: Research on learners’ difficulties can inform improvements to language lessons.

options.text: Using linguistic methods and findings to address practical language-related problems
Compiling every possible sentence into a single dictionary
Restricting language research to the mechanics of sound transmission
Avoiding practical settings in favor of isolated examples only

questions.question: A team uses evidence about learners’ difficulties to revise an English teaching programme. Which field is most directly reflected in this practical goal?
questions.explanation: The programme revision applies linguistic research to teaching. Other branches may provide evidence, but the goal of improving instruction makes the project applied.
questions.example: Lessons may be redesigned after evidence shows that students misinterpret common instructions.

options.text: Literary stylistics
Historical sound analysis
Applied linguistics
Acoustic phonetics

questions.question: A linguist examines the wording of a disputed confession in a legal case. Which application named in the lecture is the most direct match?
questions.explanation: Forensic linguistics concerns language in legal settings. The scenario involves analysing language as evidence in a case, rather than deciding the legal outcome itself.
questions.example: An analysis may examine whether the wording of a statement is clear or open to more than one interpretation.

options.text: Articulatory phonetics
Dictionary compilation
Literary stylistics
Forensic linguistics

questions.question: A researcher uses linguistic evidence to help translators make public-health messages understandable in another language. Which field best captures this practical purpose?
questions.explanation: The purpose is to improve communication through translation. Meaning, vocabulary, and context can all contribute evidence to this applied task.
questions.example: A translator may replace an unfamiliar technical expression with a clear equivalent suited to the intended readers.

options.text: Applied linguistics
Literary stylistics
Acoustic phonetics
Phonological pattern description

questions.question: Which project best demonstrates the broad scope of applied linguistics presented in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The distinguishing emphasis is the practical language-related purpose. Applied linguistics can draw on several branches and is not restricted to classroom teaching.
questions.example: Improving the clarity of official forms and improving language lessons are different applied tasks.

options.text: Using linguistic analysis to improve teaching, policy communication, translation, or courtroom language practices
Studying a poem’s structure solely to propose an interpretation of that poem
Listing grammatical patterns without considering any use for the findings
Measuring vowel frequency while deliberately excluding any practical language question

questions.question: What is the primary object of study in computational linguistics as described in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Computational linguistics investigates human languages with computational methods. A programming language may be used as a tool, but natural language remains the object being analysed or modelled.
questions.example: A researcher can use a program to analyse English sentences without treating the program’s language as the research target.

options.text: Computer programming syntax without any human-language question
Natural language investigated through computational methods and models
Computer hardware without any language-processing task
Handwritten letter shapes without any computational analysis

questions.question: A system automatically translates an Urdu sentence into English. Which field most directly addresses the computational processing involved?
questions.explanation: Automatic translation requires computational handling of natural language. Translation can also be an applied concern, but the question specifically foregrounds the automated processing.
questions.example: A translation program must produce an output that represents the source message in another language.

options.text: Language-attitude research
Literary stylistics
Articulatory phonetics
Computational linguistics

questions.question: Which pairing correctly distinguishes automatic speech recognition from artificial speech production?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists both recognizing human speech and producing artificial speech as computational areas. One deals with input, while the other creates an output signal.
questions.example: Voice typing recognizes speech; a device reading a written message aloud produces artificial speech.

options.text: Recognition studies word endings; speech production studies only paragraph links.
Recognition interprets spoken input; speech production generates a spoken output.
Recognition generates a voice; speech production records a listener’s opinion.
Recognition compiles dictionary meanings; speech production ranks regional accents.

questions.question: Which project best matches the technological aim of computational linguistics in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The technological aim concerns making computers useful for natural-language analysis and processing. The defining feature is the computational language task rather than the mere presence of a computer.
questions.example: A tool that converts spoken requests into usable instructions pursues a technological language-processing goal.

options.text: Developing a computer tool that analyses and processes natural-language input
Surveying language attitudes without a computational processing goal
Explaining a poem’s imagery without a computational method
Comparing tongue positions without using a language-processing model

questions.question: Which project best matches the lecture’s psychological aim of computational linguistics?
questions.explanation: A computational model can be used to explore how people process language. The psychological aim is understanding human processing, rather than producing a tool merely because it uses a computer.
questions.example: Researchers might ask whether a model’s difficulty with particular sentences resembles the difficulty observed in people.

options.text: Testing a computational model against patterns of human language processing
Generating clearer synthetic announcements solely for a station’s public-address system
Improving an automatic translator solely to increase its translation accuracy
Increasing a voice-typing tool’s transcription accuracy solely for its users

questions.question: What is the central focus of neurolinguistics in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Neurolinguistics investigates the neural basis of language. The lecture includes disturbances of comprehension and production associated with brain damage as one important line of evidence.
questions.example: A researcher may relate a change in language abilities to evidence about an affected brain region.

options.text: The ordering of entries in dictionaries
Language processing and representation in the brain
The social prestige of different accents
The effect of sentence repetition in literary texts

questions.question: A researcher relates changes in a patient’s language comprehension to evidence of brain injury. Which field is most directly involved?
questions.explanation: The study connects language performance with the brain. It therefore foregrounds a neural explanation rather than a social pattern or a dictionary task.
questions.example: A project can compare which language tasks are difficult after an injury without assuming that every patient has the same difficulties.

options.text: Sociolinguistics
Neurolinguistics
Lexicography
Literary stylistics

questions.question: Why does the lecture discuss disturbances of both language production and comprehension under neurolinguistics?
questions.explanation: Producing and understanding language both depend on neural processes. Studying difficulties in either can inform research, but a behavioral observation alone does not establish a precise neural explanation.
questions.example: Difficulty understanding spoken instructions and difficulty producing a sentence can motivate different language assessments.

options.text: Production belongs to the brain, but comprehension is unrelated to it.
Comprehension belongs to the brain, but production is only a social convention.
A change in language automatically identifies one exact brain location without further evidence.
Changes in either ability can provide evidence about the brain basis of language.

questions.question: How does the lecture characterize the focus of cognitive linguistics?
questions.explanation: The slide presents a perspective connecting language with cognition. It draws attention to how linguistic expressions help users organize and communicate information.
questions.example: A researcher can investigate how speakers use linguistic categories to organize what they describe.

options.text: Language as a means of organizing, processing, and conveying information
Language as a set of dictionary entries unrelated to thought
Language as a legal procedure for establishing institutional authority
Language as a speech signal studied without interpretation

questions.question: A researcher asks how linguistic categories help speakers organize information about their experience. Which approach is the closest match to the lecture’s description?
questions.explanation: The question concerns language as a resource for organizing information. This is a cognitive focus, although related work can overlap with research on meaning or mental processing.
questions.example: Researchers might examine how a general category such as “vehicle” organizes descriptions of cars and buses.

options.text: Forensic linguistics
Cognitive linguistics
Acoustic phonetics
Lexicography

questions.question: The overview names an anthropological branch without developing its definition. Which introductory description best identifies this field?
questions.explanation: Linguistic anthropology examines language within social and cultural practices. This brief definition supplies context for a field named in the overview, rather than adding a new detailed topic to the lecture.
questions.example: A researcher might study how ceremonial ways of speaking help transmit community traditions.

options.text: The measurement of speech signals without examining their cultural use
The study of language in relation to cultural practices and social life
The compilation of software commands without a question about human communication
The analysis of word endings without examining community practices
